title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling Playbook, Benchmarks and Runbooks
author: Samantha Lee
content:
Overview
--------
This document consolidates the serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling policies, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, recent release notes, known issues, and primary runbooks. It is intended for engineers on serving-runtime, infra, and SRE who operate and optimize inference hosts. The goal is to provide a single, actionable reference for diagnosing performance regressions, planning kernel/scheduler changes, and running reproducible benchmarks.

Key takeaways:
- Architecture: dispatcher, request-router, batcher, model-workers (GPU), kv-cache service, and telemetry exporters.
- Scheduling: dynamic batching + preemption policies, prioritized queues for SLO-sensitive traffic, and device-level affinity.
- Profiling: standardized trace and sampling flows using Nsight/Perf, microbench harnesses, and the internal trace-correlator.
- Benchmarks: token throughput (tokens/sec), cost-per-token, cold-start latency, and p50/p95 latency by sequence-length buckets.
- Runbooks: step-by-step procedures for high tail latency, GPU OOMs, and model quality regressions.

1. Runtime Architecture (summary)
--------------------------------
Short description: The runtime is a modular, high-throughput serving stack optimized for transformer-style autoregressive and decoder-only models. Components: 
- Request Dispatcher (grpc-proxy): receives REST/gRPC requests, authenticates, tags with routing policy, and forwards to the router.
- Smart Router: routes requests to model variants, region/capacity pools, or fallback variants based on policy. Implements rate-limiting and simple cost-based routing heuristics.
- Batchers (per-model-instance): accumulate requests into micro-batches using dynamic batching windows with max_batch and max_latency knobs.
- Model Worker (GPU process): executes tokenizer, forward pass, and streaming output. Manages KV cache, CUDA streams, and kernel selection.
- KV-Cache Service: optional network-backed prefix cache for long-context reuse across requests.
- Telemetry Exporter & Tracing: emits request traces, batch metrics, kernel timings, and GPU memory counters (via exporter sidecar).

SLOs and Targets
- Typical model SLOs (short prompts, 4\u201332 tokens): p50 < 30ms, p95 < 120ms for dedicated tier; hosted API targets are slightly higher to account for multi-tenant variance.
- Throughput targets: dependent on instance type; see Benchmarking section for measured baselines.

Ownership and Contacts
- Primary: serving-runtime team (owner: eng-serving-runtime).
- On-call: see /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks for schedule.
- Slack channel: #serving-runtime-ops.

2. Kernel selection & scheduling rationale
-----------------------------------------
Goals: minimize tail latency, maximize GPU utilization, and keep QoS (priority tiers) for latency-sensitive traffic.
Key mechanisms:
- Kernel catalog and heuristics: runtime chooses kernels per op based on sequence length, batch size, and device. Heuristics prefer fused attention kernels for short sequences and tiled matmuls for long ones.
- CUDA stream isolation: each active model-worker uses multiple CUDA streams to overlap IO, kernel compute and lightweight CPU work (tokenization/IO).
- Scheduler policies:
  - DynamicBatchingPolicy (default): waits up to max_latency_ms (config default 5ms) or until max_batch (config default 32) is reached.
  - PriorityQueuePolicy: separate queues for realtime (high-priority), default, and background (low-priority) traffic. High-priority requests bypass slow-start batch growth.
  - PreemptiveEvict: for guaranteed-tier workloads we preempt lower-priority batches after a configurable timeout (default 50ms) to meet p95 SLO.
  - AffinityPolicy: pins hot models to preferred GPUs and sets NUMA/CPU affinity for host processes to reduce PCIe transfer jitter.
- Memory/Kernel safety: kernel chooser prefers memory-conservative kernels under >80% GPU memory utilization to avoid OOM.

Configuration snippet (example)
|setting|default|description|
|---|---:|---|
|max_batch|32|Maximum requests that will be batched together|
|max_latency_ms|5|Maximum time (ms) the batcher will wait before dispatch|
|priority_queues|[realtime,default,background]|Names of priority queues|
|preempt_timeout_ms|50|Time after which low-priority work can be preempted|
|kernel_memory_threshold_pct|80|Switch to low-memory kernels if GPU memory >= this percent|

3. Profiling playbook (step-by-step)
------------------------------------
Use these steps when diagnosing a performance regression or investigating an optimization. The baseline workflow produces reproducible traces and a short actionable report.
Prerequisites: access to a profiling host (tag: profiling), credentials for telemetry, nsight/cli tools installed.

3.1 Quick checks (3\u201310 minutes)
1) Confirm alert/metric: check dashboards: serving-runtime/main-latency, batch-size-distribution, gpu-memory-usage.
2) Identify affected model(s) and pools: filter traces by model_id and pool_id.
3) Check recent deploys: list recent canary/rollouts for model variant. If a model rollout occurred within last 30 minutes, consider rollback first.

3.2 Full trace (30\u201390 minutes)
1) Enable detailed tracing for the model worker for a small percentage (1\u20135%) of traffic or replay a captured workload on a profiling host.
2) Run system-level trace:
   - Nsight Systems (recommended):
     nsys profile -o /tmp/nsys_profile --capture=cuda,cudnn,osrt --trace-fork=true --sample=cpu --duration=60s -- python -m serving_runtime.profiling.replay --workload /tmp/wl.json
   - Lightweight sample (when Nsight is unavailable): perf record -F 99 -a -g -- sleep 60
3) Collect runtime traces and correlate with telemetry (trace_id). Use trace-correlator to join batch boundaries with kernel-level timings:
   - trace-correlator --input /tmp/nsys_profile.qdrep --out /tmp/trace_summary.json --join-metrics serving-metrics://<trace_id>
4) Inspect output: identify long kernel times, host-side queuing, or large variations in batch sizes.

3.3 Microprofiling (when kernel-level regressions are suspected)
1) Use microbench harness (local):
   python tools/microbench.py --model <model> --seq-length 512 --batch-sizes 1,2,4,8 --repeat 20 --device gpu
2) Run per-kernel timing: enable kernel-timer in model worker (env: SR_KERNEL_TIMER=1) and replay microbench workload.
3) Compare to golden baseline (stored at s3://benchmarks/serving-runtime/golden/<model>/<date>).

3.4 Reporting and action
- Required fields in triage ticket: model_id, pool_id, observed p50/p95 deviation, batch-size-distribution, nsys export, microbench results, suggested mitigation (kernel/config rollback, change batching policy).
- If regression is caused by a new kernel: tag kernel owner and open an ADR if behavior requires API or config changes.

4. Benchmarking suite
---------------------
The benchmarking harness targets repeatable measurements for throughput, latency, and cold-start behavior. Benchmarks are split by model family and sequence length buckets.
Baseline hardware: H100-80GB (Apex cluster) and A100-80GB (legacy cluster).
Key measurements:
- Steady-state tokens/sec (throughput) at target p95 latency bound.
- Cost-per-token (estimated using instance hourly cost and throughput).
- Cold-start latency (time to first token for a freshly spun worker).
- Memory pressure crossover points (where kernel changes).

How to run (short)
1) Allocate benchmarking pool: ./tools/allocate_pool --cluster bench-h100 --size 4 --pool testing-bench
2) Run harness: python -m serving_runtime.bench --model gptx-medium --seq 256 --workload synthetic --duration 600 --out results/gptx-medium-256.json
3) Upload results: ./tools/upload_results --input results/*.json --bucket s3://benchmarks/serving-runtime/runs/2026-11

Interpreting results
- Compare against golden baseline using tools/compare_baselines.py. Look for >10% drop in tokens/sec or >20% increase in p95 latency as thresholds for blocking changes.

5. Release notes (recent highlights)
-----------------------------------
- 2026-11-10 (v2026.11.0) \u2014 Major
  - Added PriorityQueuePolicy and preemptive-evict to improve p95 for realtime traffic by ~30% in tests.
  - Kernel chooser now includes tiled-matmul-4k path for long sequences, reducing memory pressure for long-context models.
  - Exposed SR_KERNEL_TIMER for per-kernel microtiming.

- 2026-09-28 (v2026.09.2) \u2014 Patch
  - Fix: avoid rare CUDA launch hang impacting multi-GPU model-parallel workloads.
  - Perf: optimized attention kernel selection for batch sizes 1\u20134.

- 2026-07-12 (v2026.07.0) \u2014 Minor
  - Telemetry exporter buffer sizing defaults changed to reduce trace loss under high throughput.

Backport policy: critical correctness or stability fixes are backported to latest LTS branch. Performance improvements are staged and gated behind opt-in feature flags.

6. Known issues and mitigations
-------------------------------
1) Issue: Intermittent p95 spikes when background jobs saturate PCIe bus.
   - Symptoms: GPU kernels run with normal duration, but host-side queuing increases; batch sizes fluctuate.
   - Mitigation: Throttle background workloads, enable affinityPolicy to pin background IO to other NUMA nodes.
2) Issue: OOM in tiled kernels for long-context models after a kernel upgrade.
   - Mitigation: Set kernel_memory_threshold_pct to 85 and restart model-worker; schedule rollback of kernel package.
3) Issue: Nsight traces show long CPU-side stalls caused by Python GIL when tokenization is heavy.
   - Mitigation: Move tokenization to a lightweight Rust/Go sidecar or enable tokenization worker pool.
4) Issue: Rare CUDA driver race with H100 multi-instance GPU causing hangs under extreme concurrency.
   - Mitigation: pin to older driver (r547) on affected pools and file vendor bug with the driver team.

7. Runbooks (operational procedures)
------------------------------------
A. High p95 latency (short action checklist)
1) Scope: Identify affected models/pools on dashboard.
2) If latest deploy within 30m: rollback to previous stable variant.
3) If no deploy: capture traces (enable 1% sampling), collect nsight snapshot for 60s and microbench the model on a profiling host.
4) If GPU memory > 85%: consider draining lower-priority pools and switching to low-memory kernel.
5) Notify on-call and create post-incident triage ticket with artifacts.

B. GPU OOM (immediate)
1) Kill offending worker instance (via orchestrator) and mark node for investigation.
2) Check recent kernel rollouts or model changes.
3) If reproducible on a single model, temporarily lower max_batch and kernel_memory_threshold_pct.
4) Repro-run microbench to capture memory profile and escalate to runtime-kernel owners if needed.

C. Model quality regression (output anomalies)
1) Reproduce with eval prompt set in eval-harness.
2) If rollout triggered recently, perform canary rollback and compare golden-eval results.
3) Open a cross-team incident with applied-ml-and-evals and model-onboarding.

8. Team Wiki and operational artifacts

- Golden baselines: s3://benchmarks/serving-runtime/golden/<model>/

Appendix A \u2014 Example troubleshooting commands
-------------------------------------------
# Run microbench locally
python tools/microbench.py --model gptx-medium --seq-length 512 --batch-sizes 1 2 4 8 --repeat 20 --device gpu

# Nsight capture (recommended)
nsys profile -o /tmp/nsys_profile --capture=cuda,cudnn,osrt --trace-fork=true --sample=cpu --duration=60s -- python -m serving_runtime.profiling.replay --workload /tmp/wl.json

# Quick batcher config check via admin API
curl -s -H \"Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN\" https://admin.internal/serving/batcher/config?model=gptx-medium
